title: Read Shell Midden (15Bt10), Butler County
summary: In Butler County, the Read Shell Midden is a Late Archaic camp and cemetery dug by WPA crews from 1937 to 1939, with more than 240 burials found.
bodyMarkdown:
Long before farming came to Kentucky, Late Archaic people (roughly 3000–1000 BCE) came back to the same spots in Butler County year after year. Each visit added to a deep layer of shellfish shells, ash, broken tools and food waste. Archaeologists call these heaps shell [middens](https://grokipedia.com/page/Midden). The Read Shell Midden is one of the best-recorded in the state. It was a seasonal camp, and it was also a cemetery where families buried their dead in the same ground they had lived on.

The [Archaic period](https://grokipedia.com/page/Archaic_period_(North_America)) was a time of hunting, fishing and gathering. Groups moved through the year to follow food sources: shellfish and fish in warm months, nuts and deer in the fall. A midden used again and again shows a deep tie to one place. Burying relatives there may have helped families claim that place as theirs.

From 1937 to 1939, crews paid by the [Works Progress Administration](https://grokipedia.com/page/Works_Progress_Administration) dug the site under [William S. Webb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_S._Webb) of the University of Kentucky. New Deal relief money paid unemployed Kentuckians to do the digging, and it built much of what scholars know about the state's ancient past. The crews recorded more than 240 burials. The bones were poorly preserved, so only about 152 individuals could be removed for study. Webb published his report in 1950, and later researchers used the remains to study ancient age at death, health and population.

In 1986 the site was listed on the [National Register of Historic Places](https://npgallery.nps.gov/AssetDetail/NRIS/86000647) as part of a group of Archaic shell middens. Together they make up Kentucky's densest Archaic shell-midden landscape.

## Kentucky today

The Read Shell Midden is still a key reference for the Late Archaic in Kentucky. It's also a reminder that the WPA-era digs left records and collections that archaeologists still study today, and questions about how to treat ancestral remains with respect.
